Coriander
kôr-ē-ăn'dər
n. (a seed of the parsley kind; twice used to describe the appearance of the manna)
Greek koriannon, through Latin coriandrum. The Hebrew gad names the same small round seed, familiar in every Near Eastern kitchen and therefore the natural comparison for something no one had seen before.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Both uses describe the manna, and between them they give its look, its colour and its taste. “And the house of Israel called the name thereof Manna: and it was like coriander seed, white; and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey” (Exo 16:31). Numbers adds the further comparison to bdellium (Num 11:7). The choice of coriander is itself instructive: to describe an unprecedented thing, Scripture reaches for the most ordinary object in a household. The name the people gave it works the same way — manna, from their first question, what is it?, so that Israel ate a food whose name was a question for forty years. And it fell six mornings a week, doubled on the sixth, bred worms if hoarded, and stopped the day after they ate the old corn of the land. The Lord Jesus took up the whole account and settled its meaning: your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead; I am that bread of life.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines coriander as an annual plant, the seeds of which have a strong smell and are used in medicine and confectionery.

expand to see more

CORIANDER, n. [L. coriandrum.] A plant, the Coriandrum sativum.

The seeds are round, of an agreeable smell when dried, and used in cookery and medicine.

It was like coriander seed, white. Ex. xvi.

The green herb has a strong disagreeable scent.

Key Scripture

Exo 16:31 — "And the house of Israel called the name thereof Manna: and it was like coriander seed, white; and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey."

Exo 16:3 — "And the children of Israel said unto them, Would to God we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger."

Num 11:6 — "But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes."

Num 11:5 — "We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:"

Modern Corruption

The manna is explained away as a natural secretion of the tamarisk, and the explanation cannot account for a single one of the details Scripture actually gives.

expand to see more

The standard naturalistic account identifies manna with the sweet excretion left on tamarisk twigs by scale insects in the Sinai. It is a real substance, and it explains nothing in Exodus 16. That manna fell six days and not the seventh; that a double portion fell on the sixth day; that what was kept overnight bred worms and stank, while the sabbath portion kept sweet; that every man gathered according to his eating and, when measured, he that gathered much had nothing over and he that gathered little had no lack; that it fed some two million people for forty years across changing terrain; and that it ceased the day after they ate of the old corn of the land of Canaan. No insect keeps a sabbath. The account is either a miracle or an invention, and the tamarisk is not a middle way.

What the coriander comparison guards against is the opposite error, which is to make the miracle so exotic that it stops being food. The manna is described in the plainest kitchen terms available — the size and shape of a coriander seed, white, tasting like a honey wafer — and it had to be gathered, ground, beaten and baked. God's supernatural provision came in a form a woman could cook. That is the shape of nearly all His giving: an ordinary loaf multiplied, water made wine at a village wedding, a Saviour born in a stable and called a carpenter's son. The Lord Jesus made the manna the text of the great discourse at Capernaum, and the offence there was exactly its ordinariness — is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gad (H1407), coriander seed; with man (H4478), manna, from man hu, what is it; and tsappichith (H6838), a honey wafer.

expand to see more

Hebrew gad (H1407) — coriander; it was like coriander seed, white; Exodus 16:31, Numbers 11:7.

Hebrew man (H4478) — manna; named from the people's question, what is it; Exodus 16:15.

Hebrew tsappichith (H6838) — a flat cake or wafer; the taste of it was like wafers made with honey; Exodus 16:31.

Hebrew bedolach (H916) — bdellium; the colour comparison added in Numbers; Numbers 11:7.

Greek artos tes zoes — the bread of life; the Lord's own interpretation of the manna; John 6:35.

Usage

"“Like coriander seed, white” — an unprecedented thing described by a kitchen staple."

"“The taste of it was like wafers made with honey” — and they called it nothing at all."

"“What is it?” — a food whose name stayed a question for forty years."
